questions.title: Why does left-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserve pairwise neuron angles in OFT?
questions.question_body: In the paper, a pretrained linear layer has weights \(\mathbf{W}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}\), and OFT/BOFT form the finetuned weights as \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\) with \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) orthogonal. The authors say this preserves the pairwise angles between "neurons" (the columns of \(\mathbf{W}^0\)). I think that means for columns \(\mathbf{w}_i, \mathbf{w}_j\) of \(\mathbf{W}^0\), the cosine \(\cos\theta_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{w}_j}{\|\mathbf{w}_i\|\,\|\mathbf{w}_j\|}\) remains unchanged after mapping to \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_i, \mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_j\). Could someone show the explicit steps (with shapes) that make this true despite the forward pass being \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top\mathbf{x}\)? Also, is there any subtlety if \(\mathbf{W}^0\) has different normalization across columns?

questions.title: How exactly are butterfly components made orthogonal via the Cayley transform?
questions.question_body: The paper defines a butterfly factor \(\mathbf{B}^F(k) = \begin{bmatrix} \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{d}_1) & \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{d}_2) \\ \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{d}_3) & \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{d}_4) \end{bmatrix}\) and then says each butterfly component \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d,k)\) can be made orthogonal using the Cayley transform, effectively by parameterizing each \(2\times 2\) (or \(2b\times 2b\)) block as orthogonal. I am confused about the mapping between the diagonal-vector parameterization in \(\mathbf{B}^F(k)\) and a blockwise Cayley parameterization. Do we ignore the diagonal-vector form and instead directly parameterize each \(2\times 2\) (or \(2b\times 2b\)) nonzero block using \(\mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}^\top = -\mathbf{Q}\)? If so, what exactly are those blocks (an explicit index-level description would help), and how do we reconcile this with the notation in Equation (1)?

questions.title: Deriving the BOFT parameter count: why is it \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\)?
questions.question_body: The paper claims BOFT\((m,b)\) uses \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) effective trainable parameters for a layer of size \(d \times n\). Could someone derive this count carefully? Specifically: (1) how many independent degrees of freedom does each \(2b\times 2b\) orthogonal block contribute under this butterfly sparsity pattern, (2) how many such blocks appear per butterfly component at dimension \(d\), and (3) how do constraints implied by orthogonality and the product structure reduce the naive parameter count to the stated formula?

questions.title: In the information-transmission view, what are “free edges” and why are \(d\) edges per level pair considered non-trainable?
questions.question_body: The paper says that for each factor \(\mathbf{B}_i\) to be full rank (and hence potentially orthogonal), we need at least \(d\) edges to form a bijection between levels, and these \(d\) edges "are not trainable (e.g., for a \(d\times d\) orthogonal with \(d\) nonzeros, they can only be \(\pm 1\))." I am not following this. What precisely is a "free edge" versus a non-trainable edge here? Orthogonal matrices with exactly one nonzero per row/column are signed permutations, but once we allow more nonzeros per row/column the values need not be \(\pm 1\). How does this translate into a parameter-counting rule for the product of sparse orthogonal factors?

questions.title: Why does BOFT(1, b) recover block-diagonal OFT and BOFT(1, d) recover full OFT?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BOFT\((1,b)\) reduces to block-diagonal OFT with block size \(b\), and BOFT\((1,d)\) equals the original OFT with a dense \(d\times d\) orthogonal matrix. Could someone show this explicitly from the definition of the block butterfly component \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b(d, 2)\)? In particular, how does a single butterfly component with block size \(b\) equal a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix, and why does choosing \(b=d\) remove sparsity altogether?

questions.title: How is BOFT defined when \(d\) is not a power of two?
questions.question_body: The butterfly recursion is described for \(d = 2^N\). In practice, transformer layers often have dimensions like \(d=768\) or \(d=4096\), which are not exact powers of two or decompose into mixed small primes. What is the exact construction used when \(d\) is not a power of two? Do you pad, use mixed-radix butterfly components, or adopt the "pixelated" generalization cited? A small worked example for, say, \(d=6\) or \(d=12\) would be very helpful.

questions.title: Are explicit permutation matrices part of BOFT, or is the butterfly pattern achieved without extra permutations?
questions.question_body: Many fast transforms use permutations (bit-reversal, stride permutations) between butterfly stages. The paper mentions that nonzero patterns of butterfly components are permutations of the \(k=2\) case. Are these permutations: (1) fixed, hard-coded reindexings, (2) represented explicitly as learned or fixed permutation matrices, or (3) implicitly realized by how block-diagonal factors are arranged? An explicit statement of whether BOFT includes separate permutation matrices in the product would clarify both expressivity and implementation.

questions.title: Unpacking the expressivity theorem: how does the kaleidoscope product span the full orthogonal group?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims BOFT is more expressive than block-diagonal OFT and references a product of butterfly matrices and their transposes (a kaleidoscope hierarchy) that can represent all \(d\times d\) orthogonal matrices when \(m_1 = m_2 = \log d\), \(b_1=b_2=2\), and \(l=d-1\). Could someone provide a proof sketch or an explicit reference explaining why the alternating product \(\mathbf{B}_{d-1,1}(d)\mathbf{B}^\top_{d-1,2}(d)\cdots\mathbf{B}_{1,1}(d)\mathbf{B}^\top_{1,2}(d)\) spans all of \(\mathcal{O}(d)\)? Also, does this require any extra permutations between butterfly factors?

questions.title: Does left-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserve all singular values, not just the spectral norm?
questions.question_body: The paper emphasizes that BOFT preserves the spectral norm because \(\mathbf{W}^0 = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top\) becomes \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top\) with \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{U}\) still orthogonal. But then all singular values (not just the largest) are unchanged, right? If so, is there a reason the text highlights only the spectral norm and not the full singular value spectrum being preserved?

questions.title: How should BOFT’s multiplicative Dropout be scaled to preserve expected activations?
questions.question_body: The proposed multiplicative Dropout randomly replaces a subset of \(2b\times 2b\) orthogonal blocks in some butterfly components by identity. In standard Dropout we scale by \(1/(1-p)\) to preserve the expected activation. Here, should each retained block be scaled to keep \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}(m,b)] = \mathbf{I}\) (or some other target), or is no rescaling intended? If no rescaling is used, what is the intuition for why this does not bias training or harm stability?

questions.title: What is the computational overhead of BOFT during training, asymptotically and in practice?
questions.question_body: In training, BOFT forms \(\mathbf{R}(m,b)\) as a product of \(m\) sparse orthogonal butterfly components and applies it to the left of \(\mathbf{W}^0\). What is the per-layer complexity to multiply \(\mathbf{R}(m,b)\) by a vector and by \(\mathbf{W}^0\) during forward/backward passes? Asymptotically, is it \(\mathcal{O}(dm)\) per application (e.g., \(\mathcal{O}(d\log d)\) for the butterfly case)? In practice, how does this overhead compare to LoRA with rank \(r\) in typical transformer sizes, and are there recommended ways to implement \(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{x}\) efficiently without materializing dense matrices?

questions.title: How are OFT/BOFT related to LoRA in the small-update regime?
questions.question_body: With the Cayley parameterization \(\mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) and \(\|\mathbf{Q}\|\) small, we can expand \(\mathbf{R} \approx \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{Q} + 2\mathbf{Q}^2 + \cdots\). Then \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0 - \mathbf{W}^0 \approx 2\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{W}^0\) to first order. Is there a way to interpret this as a low-rank update like LoRA if \(\mathbf{Q}\) is additionally constrained to be low-rank? Conversely, can LoRA be seen as a special case of OFT/BOFT under some constraints and reparameterizations?

questions.title: Why can’t a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix approximate classic transforms like the DFT?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that block-diagonal OFT introduces undesirable inductive bias and cannot approximate classic linear transforms (e.g., DFT), whereas butterfly-structured BOFT can. Could someone formalize this limitation? Is it because any block-diagonal matrix preserves independent subspaces that cannot mix coordinates across blocks, and the DFT is dense and highly mixing? A short proof or clear argument would help.

questions.title: Clarifying the edge-count example: how does a butterfly on \(d=4\) achieve dense connectivity with 8 edges?
questions.question_body: The paper states that in the information-transmission view, a naive dense connection for \(d=4\) needs 12 edges, the example factorization uses 10 edges, and a butterfly network uses 8 edges. Could someone explicitly draw or list the edges for the \(d=4\) butterfly case across all levels, and show how they imply that every source node reaches every sink node? I am trying to match this to the corresponding matrix sparsity patterns.

questions.title: Where does the formula \(m = \log\tfrac{2d}{b}\) come from for BOFT to produce a dense \(\mathbf{R}\)?
questions.question_body: The text says BOFT\((\log\tfrac{2d}{b}, b)\) with block butterfly factors yields a dense orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\). Could someone derive this \(m\) as a function of \(d\) and \(b\) from the recursive definition of the block butterfly components? A step-by-step argument showing that after \(m\) stages all input coordinates can influence all outputs would be great.

questions.title: Is \(\mathbf{R}\) shared across layers or is there one \(\mathbf{R}\) per layer?
questions.question_body: In one place the paper contrasts BOFT with "butterfly-based sparse training" by stating that BOFT transforms weights with layer-shared weight matrices. Elsewhere, OFT is described as learning an orthogonal matrix for a given layer. I am confused: in practice, do we learn a distinct \(\mathbf{R}\) for each layer (e.g., per attention projection and MLP matrix), or is a single \(\mathbf{R}\) shared across multiple layers? Clarifying this for LLMs and ViTs would help interpret parameter counts and results.

questions.title: Numerical stability of Cayley parameterization in BOFT: how is \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) computed safely?
questions.question_body: The Cayley transform requires inverting \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\). Even though \(\mathbf{Q}\) is skew-symmetric, \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\) could become ill-conditioned during training. What implementation details ensure stability? For example: (1) is \(\mathbf{Q}\) implicitly blocked into independent \(2\times 2\) (or \(2b\times 2b\)) blocks so inverses are cheap and stable, (2) is there a trust-region or norm constraint on \(\mathbf{Q}\), or (3) do you use an alternative like the exponential map \(\exp(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^\top)\)?

questions.title: What exactly is the “weight interpolation” property of BOFT and how is it computed?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an "intriguing weight interpolation" (referring to a figure) that comes from the matrix factorization. Could someone explain what is being interpolated? Is it an interpolation along the product path of \(\mathbf{R}(m,b) = \prod_{i=1}^m \tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b_{(d,i)}\), e.g., linearly interpolating between partial products, or something like geodesic interpolation on the orthogonal group? How is this property used in practice (e.g., for model selection or regularization)?

questions.title: Which weight matrices in a transformer receive BOFT, and how are dimension mismatches handled?
questions.question_body: For transformers, a layer may contain several linear maps with shapes like \(d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}\), \(d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}\), and \(d_{\text{model}} \times d_k\) for Q/K/V. Since BOFT left-multiplies a \(d\times d\) orthogonal matrix, do we set \(d\) to the row dimension of each weight and learn a separate \(\mathbf{R}\) per matrix? If so, how do you handle cases where some matrices share the same \(d\) and others do not? Are there any tied \(\mathbf{R}\) parameters across Q/K/V within a layer?

questions.title: Does BOFT still produce a dense \(\mathbf{R}\) when \(b=2\) but \(m < \log d\)?
questions.question_body: The text states that using the butterfly (\(b=2\), \(m=\log d\)) yields a dense \(\mathbf{R}\). What happens if we choose \(m < \log d\)? Is \(\mathbf{R}\) then guaranteed to be sparse, or merely less expressive (but potentially still dense)? If it is sparse, can you characterize the resulting sparsity pattern?

questions.title: Is there a lower bound showing \(\Omega(d\log d)\) nonzeros (or parameters) are necessary for dense connectivity via sparse orthogonal products?
questions.question_body: The paper motivates BOFT via the information-transmission view and argues that butterfly structures achieve dense connectivity with \(\mathcal{O}(d\log d)\) edges/parameters. Are there known lower bounds (perhaps from network theory or rearrangeable networks) that show \(\Omega(d\log d)\) is unavoidable to achieve all-to-all mixing under orthogonality constraints, or at least necessary in some reasonable model? A reference would help justify the near-optimality of the butterfly choice.
